Weight new TLS races by each provider\'s peak acknowledged-byte rate relative to its advertised bandwidth. With hard affinity enabled, low measured donors yield to the race. Existing connections and explicit pins stay fixed

A site\'s new connections stay on the exit its earlier ones already use, even past the flow cap, so a busy site keeps one egress IP. The cap still limits which exits collect new sites. Off restores the strict cap
How long a provider still acknowledging traffic may return nothing before it is dropped. Off keeps them until they stop acknowledging
Connections lost per provider failure. Lower is better
How long the stall probe waits for an answer before convicting. Off derives half the stall bar
When an exit stalls, ping it once before convicting. A congested but alive exit answers and keeps its flows; a dead one is still dropped. Off convicts on the stall bar
Liveness pings fired at stalled exits; acquitted ones answered and were kept, the removals the probe prevented
Keeps a site on one exit when its hostname is not visible
Drop an exit that has established nothing sooner when two sibling exits are receiving. Off waits the full 30s connect bar
When a provider can\'t reach a site, move the connection to another exit instead of letting it hang
Times a provider reported it could not open the upstream connection
Failing dials and survived verdicts push a provider down the ranking within a second; promotion back needs clean minutes and a proven connect
How many providers a window expansion pings and ranks per slot it needs, keeping the best. 1 evaluates exactly what it needs
Total since reset, so runs of different lengths compare
Flows moved to a warm exit inside a removal; accepted means the server took the path change without a re-dial
How many of those failures were quietly moved instead of hanging
How often a connecting flow re-checks an empty window, so the first request leaves right after the first exit lands. Off waits the 2s retry pace

Assign each new connection to the exit its IP or domain already uses. Off is the default: every ordinary fresh connection reaches the provider race. Existing connections and explicit pins always stay fixed

A quarantined exit keeps its own sites\' new connections through the early bench, when the verdict is least proven, so a bench does not split the site\'s egress IP. New sites still avoid it. Off scatters them

How long into a bench a site\'s new connections keep following their exit — early benches are usually false alarms; one that lasts is trending toward removal and stops collecting flows. Off scatters immediately
How often one line summarizing live state is written to the log for later forensics. Off silences it; shorter spots a transition, longer keeps more buffer
Uses whichever family connects first, and routes around one that fails after connecting.
Control-plane connections use IPv4 only. Turn this off on an IPv6-only network.
Control-plane connections use IPv6 only. Turn this off if the app cannot reach the server.
Extra silent destinations required per this many flows before a busy exit can be benched on soft evidence: a 24-flow exit at 8 needs 3 silent sites, not 2. Off keeps the flat minimum
Transport and window internals. Very large logs
There is no device to read the log level from yet. Sign in first
Contract accounting and per-packet block decisions. Includes destination IP addresses
At Verbose and above the logs contain the destination IP addresses and ports of the traffic you send. Use “Export redacted logs” to share them; the raw bundle should not leave this device.
Logs are recording your real traffic
Losing an exit kills every connection on it. Lower spreads the damage; a site may then use more than one exit IP
No provider failures yet. Stall an exit below to cause one.
What a provider failure costs. Reset, run a test, read back.
How many distinct destinations must be silent before an exit is convicted on no-receive, so one dead site cannot remove a working exit. Off lets a single destination convict
Qualify exits by dialing real sites through them. An answer proves the exit; silence never counts against it
How many health sites one qualification pass dials through an exit. 0 probes the entire embedded list; a smaller number rotates through it in blocks
How long a qualification probe waits for an answer. Off uses the built-in 4s. It only bounds waiting for proof, it never convicts
Re-pin established QUIC flows to a live exit inside the removal instead of tearing them down
From an exit dying to that site answering again
How many verdict removals are allowed per window before the rest are deferred; a burst is more likely one local cause than many failures. Off removes without limit
The window the removal limit is counted over. Off (like a limit of 0) turns the breaker off
Removals the storm breaker held back after a correlated burst
How long verdicts stay held after a detected suspend, giving transports time to re-register. Off uses the built-in 5s
How much timer overshoot reads as the phone being suspended rather than an exit stalling, so a resumed phone does not convict every exit at once. Off disables it
Host suspends the detector caught, each one a batch of verdicts held instead of executed on a just-resumed phone
How long an exit may stop delivering before it is dropped. Off waits 30s
Moves later connections onto the exit the first one already uses
Ambiguous verdicts bench an exit instead of tearing down its flows; removal needs sustained evidence or an empty exit
Size each window one exit beyond its target so a replacement is already connected. Off waits until a loss to backfill
How long retransmits are held before one is released. Off waits 30s
How long a TCP connection may sit idle. Off uses the UDP bound
How long a non-TCP flow may sit idle before it is reaped
Tells DNS and QUIC the path is gone instead of going silent
How long the whole tunnel may be silent before provider verdicts are held as inadmissible. 0 convicts as before
Convictions withheld because the phone\'s own uplink, not the provider, was silent (uplink / transport)

While the VPN is connected, IPv6 is routed through URnetwork like IPv4. Outbound SMTP on TCP port 25 bypasses the VPN, even when the kill switch is on, which may expose your local public IP to those mail servers. SMTP on ports 465 and 587 stays in the VPN and must establish TLS.

When the kill switch is off, traffic that URnetwork safety rules keep off the network, such as unrecognized encrypted protocols, bypasses the VPN and uses your local public IP. With the kill switch on, that traffic is blocked.
